channel.title: Pier — Blog
channel.description: Practical writing on legacy websites, FTP, MySQL and AI-assisted edits.

item.title: Diffing two SFTP trees: when 'nothing changed' isn't true
item.description: A Saturday-morning ticket. The client swears nothing changed since Friday. Three shell commands that find the one file that actually did, and the diff to paste back.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: wp-login.php brute force: the .htaccess block that works
item.description: The bots have been hammering wp-login.php every two seconds for three days. Here is the .htaccess block that stops them and the reason it does not break the dashboard.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: AI-assisted SQL: when to trust the suggested JOIN clause
item.description: AI will hand you a six-table JOIN in two seconds. Half of them are right. Here is how to tell which half before you press run on production.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: 9GB site restore: a partial dump and three FTP shards
item.description: An afternoon spent stitching a 9GB WordPress site back together from one truncated mysqldump and three half-broken FTP backups. Here is the restore log.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Legacy maintenance pricing: surviving the 'tiny fix' trap
item.description: The third 'just one tiny fix' on a 2017 WordPress site is where freelancers quietly go broke. A retainer model that bills risk, not keystrokes.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Database as source of truth: refactor the data, not the code
item.description: You inherit a 14-year-old WordPress site. You pull the repo, grep for the broken behaviour, find nothing. The real logic is a 4 KB row in wp_options.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Fake plugin updates in wp-content: seven signatures to audit
item.description: A practical audit for spotting fake plugin updates and supply-chain malware inside wp-content. Seven signatures, with the grep and SQL to actually run.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Magento 2 indexer stuck: recovery without losing orders
item.description: A stuck Magento 2 indexer turns checkout into a minefield: wrong prices, missing products, ghost stock. Here is the recovery sequence that protects the orders already in flight.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Reading PHP error logs like bloodwork: a triage field guide
item.description: A 16:47 Friday message: site is throwing 500s, sometimes. You SSH in, tail the log, see eight hundred lines of red. This is how to triage them in order.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: 40GB wp_options autoload: the night we hit 800ms TTFB
item.description: A Loom link at 23:41, a homepage TTFB over eight seconds, and a wp_options table that had quietly grown to 40GB. The fix was three SQL statements and a long night.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Recovering a corrupted MyISAM table: incident walkthrough
item.description: A WooCommerce wp_options table crashed on a shared host at 23:41. Ninety minutes, no SSH, only phpMyAdmin and FTP. Here's the incident in order.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: WooCommerce checkout audit: hunting the 2.3s plugin
item.description: A Loom from a Dutch agency: WooCommerce checkout hanging three seconds on every postcode change. Here is the twenty-minute audit that finds the plugin.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Self-hosting client work: a small studio's case for owning the dock
item.description: A three-person studio runs eleven legacy sites. The argument for self-hosting the tooling around that work, instead of renting it, gets stronger every quarter.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Reading inherited .htaccess files: a fundamentals guide
item.description: Inherited a site whose .htaccess starts with three commented blocks of dead RewriteRules in Dutch? Read it block by block. This is the order we use.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: PHP 5.6 to PHP 8.2 in one weekend: the realistic version
item.description: The Loom landed at 23:41 on a Friday. Forty-eight hours to take a 14-year-old PHP codebase from 5.6 to 8.2. Here is the actual order it broke in.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Retiring jQuery from a legacy theme: a working playbook
item.description: Most legacy themes still ship jQuery for two lines of code: a hamburger toggle and a smooth scroll. Here is how we retire it without spending a Saturday on rollbacks.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: AI-suggested edits: a four-step check before you apply
item.description: The chat returns a one-line SQL diff you didn't write and only half recognize. Before you apply it on a live site, run it through four steps.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Custom PHP intranet migration: off Windows 2008 in a weekend
item.description: An undocumented custom PHP intranet, a Windows 2008 box being pulled Monday, and one weekend. Here is the inventory, the breakages, and the cutover.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Joomla 3 to Joomla 5: template overrides that survive
item.description: Most Joomla 3 overrides are sixty percent salvageable. The other forty percent will silently break your site. Here is the rescue order we use on real client sites.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: CMS identification by filesystem: a short field guide
item.description: You inherit an FTP login, no documentation, and 20 minutes before the client call. The five places to look that name a CMS before you open a single PHP file.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Cron jobs over FTP: auditing a server you just inherited
item.description: A site lands in your lap with an FTP credential and a database dump. Somewhere in there, jobs are firing on a schedule. You need to know which ones, before one breaks at 03:00 on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Legacy site manifests: a 20-minute audit blueprint
item.description: You inherit a 9-year-old WordPress site at 4pm Friday. By 4:20 you should have a manifest that tells the next person, or you in six months, what's actually running.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Reviving a dead WordPress site: a 90-minute playbook
item.description: A Dutch agency owner sent a Loom at 23:41: white screen, no logs, no SSH. Ninety minutes later the cart was live. Here is the order we work in.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Drupal session token leaks: three patterns and the fixes
item.description: An admin getting silently logged out is rarely a flaky cookie. On legacy Drupal sites it usually means the session token is being copied out of a referrer log or a cached page.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: phpMyAdmin alternatives in 2026: when a native client wins
item.description: phpMyAdmin still ships with every cPanel on earth. That doesn't make it the right place to run an UPDATE against 180,000 wp_postmeta rows at five past eleven on a Friday.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Spotting a hacked WordPress install: a 5-minute audit
item.description: You have FTP, the database password, and maybe five minutes before the client wakes up. Here is the audit that gets you to a verdict, in roughly that order.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: WordPress without the dashboard: why some agencies live in the FTP
item.description: A look at why working WordPress agencies bypass wp-admin entirely and run their day from a file tree, a SQL prompt and a tail on the error log.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Reading raw .sql dumps without importing: a CLI playbook
item.description: A 3 GB backup lands in Slack and the client wants to know if one row is in there. The CLI workflow for reading raw .sql dumps without importing them.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Backups that aren't really backups: a seven-point audit
item.description: An agency lead sent a Loom at 23:41: the restore file was 11 MB, the database is 4.7 GB. Here's how that happens, and how to make sure it doesn't to you.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial

item.title: Inline CSS and embedded fonts: 2010s habits that aged well
item.description: Eleven years on, the parts of a 2014 WordPress theme still doing useful work are the ones we used to mock: inline CSS, self-hosted fonts, plain JavaScript.
item.dc:creator: Pier editorial
